title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker
ru: Молодой юрист едет в Трансильванию к загадочному графу — и вскоре тень вампира падает на Англию

chapters.title: Chapter 1. Jonathan Harker's Journal: The Road to the Castle
chapters.text:
Jonathan Harker's Journal

3 May, Bistritz. I left Munich on the night train and have been travelling east ever since. The further I go, the older the world seems. The trains run late, the villages look like pictures in a history book, and the women wear wide white skirts and bright scarves. Last night I had chicken cooked with red pepper for dinner, and I must ask Mina for the recipe. I am keeping this journal in shorthand so that I can tell her everything when I get home.

My business here is simple enough. I am a young solicitor — a lawyer who deals with property and contracts — and my employer, Mr Hawkins, has sent me to Transylvania to see a nobleman, Count Dracula. The Count has bought an old house near London, called Carfax, and I am bringing him the papers.

4 May. A strange thing happened this morning. When the landlady of the hotel heard where I was going, her face went white.

“Must you go?” she asked. “Oh, young sir, must you go? Do you know what day it is? Tonight is the eve of St George's Day. At midnight all the evil things in the world will have full power.”

I told her, as kindly as I could, that I had business to do and could not wait. She went down on her knees and begged me to stay. When she saw it was useless, she took a small crucifix from her own neck and put it round mine. “For your mother's sake,” she said, and hurried out of the room.

I have always thought such things a little foolish, but I could not refuse an old woman who meant so well. And yet, strangely, I feel safer with it round my neck.

The coach left that afternoon. A small crowd had gathered at the inn door, and as I climbed in, they all made the sign of the cross, pointed two fingers at me and muttered something. I asked a fellow passenger what they were saying. He did not want to answer, but at last he told me one of the words. It meant “vampire”.

We drove for hours through wild, beautiful country — green hills, dark forests and great grey mountains. Then the sun went down, the air grew cold, and the passengers became nervous. A woman pressed a dried rose into my hand. Someone else gave me garlic. Nobody would look me in the eye.

At about eleven we reached the Borgo Pass, high in the mountains, where I was to be met. Our driver kept checking his watch. “There is no one here,” he said in German. “The gentleman is not expected after all. He must come on with us to Bukovina and return tomorrow.”

But as he spoke, our horses began to scream and kick, and a carriage with four black horses came up behind us out of the darkness. Its driver was a tall man with a long brown beard and a great black hat that hid his face. When he turned towards our lamps, I saw that his eyes shone red. His lips were very red too, over teeth that were sharp and as white as ivory.

“You are early tonight, my friend,” he said to our driver.

“The English gentleman was in a hurry,” the man answered. His voice was shaking.

“That is why, I suppose, you wished him to go on to Bukovina,” said the stranger, and smiled. “You cannot deceive me, my friend. I know too much, and my horses are swift.”

He held out a hand to help me into his carriage, and it closed on my arm like a steel trap. He was terribly strong. Behind me I heard one of the passengers whisper a line from an old German poem: “For the dead travel fast.”

The strange driver turned his head. “He is right,” he said quietly, and smiled again.

What followed was like a bad dream. We climbed for hours through the dark. Dogs howled in the farms below, and then, from the mountains all around, came a longer and wilder howling. Wolves. Our horses shook with fear, but the driver said a few words to them, and they grew calm at once.

Once, when the carriage stopped, I saw something that froze my blood. We were surrounded by a ring of wolves, with white teeth and red tongues hanging out, their long thin bodies silver in the moonlight. The driver stood in the road and raised his long arms, as if he were pushing something away. One by one, the wolves went back into the trees.

At last we drove into the courtyard of a huge ruined castle. Its tall black windows showed no light at all. The driver put my bags down beside a great old door studded with iron nails, jumped back onto his seat and was gone.

I stood alone in the silence. There was no bell and no knocker. What sort of place had I come to? What sort of man was my client?

Then I heard heavy footsteps inside, the rattle of chains, and the slow grinding of a great key as it turned in the lock.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. Jonathan Harker's Journal: The Children of the Night
chapters.text:
Jonathan Harker's Journal (continued)

The door swung back. Inside stood a tall old man, clean-shaven except for a long white moustache, and dressed in black from head to foot. He held an old silver lamp, and its flame threw long, trembling shadows across the stone walls.

“Welcome to my house!” he said in excellent English, though with a strange accent. “Enter freely and of your own will!”

He did not step forward to meet me. He stood as still as a statue until I had crossed the doorway. Then he moved quickly and took my hand in a grip so strong that I almost cried out. His hand was as cold as ice — more like the hand of a dead man than a living one.

“Count Dracula?” I asked.

He bowed. “I am Dracula, and I welcome you, Mr Harker, to my house. Come in. The night air is cold, and you will need food and rest.”

He carried my bags himself — there were no servants anywhere — up a winding staircase to a bedroom where a log fire was burning. In the next room supper was waiting. The Count did not eat. “I have dined already,” he said, “and I never take supper.” He sat by the fire and watched me while I ate.

I had a good look at him then. His face was strong and proud, with a thin, high nose and thick eyebrows that almost met in the middle. His mouth was hard and rather cruel, and his sharp white teeth rested on lips that were surprisingly red for a man of his age. When he put his hands on his knees, I noticed that they were broad, with short thick fingers, and — strangest of all — there were hairs growing in the centre of the palms. The nails were long and cut to a sharp point.

Once he leaned towards me and his hand touched mine. I could not stop myself from shivering. His breath smelt foul, and a terrible feeling of sickness came over me. He must have noticed, because he drew back with a grim smile.

Outside, from the valley far below, came the howling of many wolves. The Count's eyes shone.

“Listen to them,” he said softly. “The children of the night. What music they make!” Then he saw my face and added, “Ah, sir, you people who live in cities cannot understand the feelings of the hunter.”

7 May. The Count was away all day and appeared only after sunset. We spent the evening talking. He has a wonderful library full of English books, newspapers and even railway timetables, and he asked me hundreds of questions about London: about its streets, its people, and how a stranger could live there without being noticed. When I described Carfax — an old stone house with high walls, a dark pond and a ruined chapel, next door to a private lunatic asylum — he was delighted.

“I am glad that it is old and big,” he said. “I myself come from an old family, and to live in a new house would kill me. Besides, I love the shade and the shadow, and I like to be alone with my thoughts.”

He spoke proudly of his family's ancient wars against the Turks, as if he had been there himself. We sat talking until dawn. When the first cock crowed, he jumped up as if surprised. “Why, it is morning again!” he said, and left me at once.

8 May. Something is wrong in this place, and I must write it down.

This morning I was shaving by the window, using the little mirror from my bag. Suddenly a hand touched my shoulder and I heard the Count's voice: “Good morning.” I jumped and cut myself slightly. But this is the strange thing. I had not seen him come in. The mirror showed the whole room behind me — and there was nobody in it. The Count was standing right beside me, yet in the glass there was no sign of him at all.

Then he saw the blood on my chin. His eyes blazed with a sort of devilish fury, and his hand shot out towards my throat. I pulled back, and his fingers touched the string of beads that held the landlady's crucifix. At once he changed. The fury disappeared so quickly that I could hardly believe it had been there.

“Take care,” he said, “take care how you cut yourself. It is more dangerous than you think in this country.” Then he picked up the mirror. “And this is the miserable thing that has done the damage. Away with it!” He opened the heavy window and threw it out. It smashed into a thousand pieces on the stones of the courtyard far below.

After breakfast — I have still never seen him eat or drink — I went exploring. The castle stands on the very edge of a cliff. A stone dropped from my window would fall a thousand feet before it hit anything.

I tried the doors. Doors, doors, doors everywhere, and every one of them locked and bolted. Except for the windows high in the castle walls, there is no way out.

The castle is a prison, and I am a prisoner.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Jonathan Harker's Journal: The Three Sisters
chapters.text:
Jonathan Harker's Journal (continued)

15 May. Last night I was leaning out of my window, looking at the moon, when I noticed the Count's head coming out of a window below mine. Then his whole body slowly came out, and he began to crawl down the castle wall, face down, over that terrible drop, with his black cloak spreading around him like great wings. He moved downwards quickly, just as a lizard moves along a wall.

What sort of man is this? Or what sort of creature that only looks like a man?

16 May. While the Count was out, I found a door that was not really locked, only stuck. Behind it was a part of the castle where ladies must have lived long ago. The Count had warned me never to fall asleep anywhere except in my own room. But I was tired, the place felt peaceful, and I lay down on an old sofa.

I was not alone. In the moonlight stood three young women. Two were dark, with high noses like the Count's and eyes that seemed almost red. The third was fair, with golden hair and eyes like pale blue jewels. Strangely, they threw no shadows on the floor. They whispered together and then laughed — a sweet, musical laugh, but hard, like the ringing of glass.

“Go on!” said one of the dark ones to the fair one. “You are first, and we shall follow.”

I lay still, watching through half-closed eyes, sick with fear and yet — I am ashamed to write it — full of a strange, burning desire. The fair girl knelt and bent over me. I could feel her breath on my neck, and I heard the soft, wet sound of her tongue as she licked her lips. Her sharp teeth touched my throat. I closed my eyes and waited.

Suddenly the Count was in the room. I had never imagined such anger. He seized the fair woman by the neck and threw her across the room.

“How dare you touch him, any of you?” he said in a low, terrible voice. “This man belongs to me! When I am done with him, you may kiss him as much as you like. Now go!”

“Are we to have nothing tonight?” asked one of them, pointing at a bag he had thrown on the floor. It moved, as if something alive were inside. I heard a low cry, like the cry of a child who could hardly breathe. The women closed round it, and I fainted with horror.

I woke up in my own bed.

19 May. Tonight the Count politely made me write three letters to Mina and Mr Hawkins, saying that I would soon be leaving. He told me to date them 12 June, 19 June and 29 June. Now I understand. He knows exactly how long I have to live.

24 June. A few nights ago a woman ran into the courtyard and threw herself against the castle door. “Monster, give me my child!” she screamed. From somewhere high above, the Count called out in a harsh, metallic voice, and from far and wide came the howling of wolves. Then the woman's cries stopped.

Today the Szgany — a wandering people of the mountains who serve the Count — arrived with carts and began loading great wooden boxes. Fifty of them. I know now what he is planning. He is going to London, to Carfax, to live among millions of people, where he can feed as he pleases.

25 June. I have done a mad thing. Since the Count goes out by the window, I decided to go in by the window. In daylight I climbed out and crept along the wall to his room. It was empty except for a heap of gold coins, hundreds of years old. A heavy door led down a stone staircase to a ruined chapel, and there, among the broken graves, stood the fifty boxes, filled with fresh earth. In one of them lay the Count.

He was neither dead nor asleep. His eyes were open and stony. There was no pulse, no breath. Yet he looked younger than before. His white hair and moustache had turned dark grey, his cheeks were full, and drops of fresh blood shone on his red lips. He lay there like a fat leech — one of those little creatures that suck blood — swollen and heavy with it.

I took a shovel that the workmen had left and struck at that hateful face. But the head turned, the eyes looked straight into mine with all their terrible power, and the shovel only cut a deep wound in his forehead. Then the lid fell shut. I heard the Szgany coming, singing, and I ran.

30 June. They have gone, and the Count with them. I am alone in the castle with those three women. Mina is a woman too, but there is nothing in common between her and them. They are devils.

I will not stay. I shall take some of the gold and climb down the wall, further than I have ever gone. Better to die on the rocks than to wait here for them.

Goodbye, all! Mina!

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Letters: Three Proposals and a Ship in the Storm
chapters.text:
Letter from Miss Lucy Westenra to Miss Mina Murray

24 May

My dearest Mina,

Three proposals in one day! Isn't it awful? I feel sorry, really and truly sorry, for two of the poor fellows.

The first, just before lunch, was Dr John Seward, the clever young doctor who runs the lunatic asylum. He tried to be very calm, but he kept playing with a little knife the whole time, and it made me so nervous I almost screamed. When I said there was someone else, he only took my hands and said he hoped I would be happy.

The second came after lunch: Mr Quincey Morris, the American from Texas. When I cried and told him I loved someone else, he said, “That's a brave girl. It's better to be late for a chance of winning you than to be in time for any other girl in the world.” Then he kissed my hand and walked out with a smile, and I cried like a baby.

And the third — well, I needn't tell you about number three, need I? Arthur Holmwood. Oh, Mina, I am so happy. Why can't they let a girl marry three men, or as many as want her, and save all this trouble? But I mustn't say such things.

Your ever-loving Lucy

Dr Seward's Diary (kept on phonograph)

25 May. Feel low today. Cannot eat, cannot rest. Lucy has refused me. The only cure is work, so I went down among my patients and spent the afternoon with R. M. Renfield, aged fifty-nine. He is the strangest case I have ever had.

He catches flies and eats them. When I told him it was disgusting, he answered quite calmly that flies were full of life, and that their life gave life to him. Then he started keeping spiders and feeding his flies to them. Then he got some sparrows and fed them the spiders. This morning the attendant found feathers on his floor and blood on his lips. He had eaten the birds raw. Afterwards he asked me, very politely, for a kitten.

“A nice little playful kitten,” he said, “that I can play with, and teach, and feed — and feed — and feed!”

I said no. He begged for a cat, a big one, and when I refused again, a look of pure murder came into his face. I have invented a name for his madness: he is zoophagous — an eater of living things. He wants to take in as many lives as he can, from the smallest upwards. What will he want after cats, I wonder?

Mina Murray's Journal

24 July, Whitby. Lucy met me at the station. Whitby is a beautiful little town. High on the East Cliff stand the ruins of an old abbey and a churchyard full of ancient gravestones. There is a seat there, looking out to sea, which is my favourite spot in the world. An old sailor, Mr Swales, often joins us. He says half the graves are empty, because the men they belong to were lost at sea.

There has been no letter from Jonathan for a whole month. I am so anxious.

Lucy is well, but she has started walking in her sleep again, as she did when she was a child. Her mother has asked me to lock our bedroom door every night.

From a newspaper cutting, pasted into Mina's journal

8 August. Yesterday one of the most sudden and violent storms that anyone can remember struck the coast at Whitby. In the middle of it, a foreign ship was seen racing towards the harbour with all her sails up. It seemed certain that she would be smashed on the rocks. Then a great wave lifted her, and she shot into the harbour and ran up onto the sand beneath the East Cliff.

The moment she touched the shore, an enormous dog leapt up from below deck, jumped onto the sand and ran straight up the cliff towards the churchyard.

The coastguards who climbed aboard found a dreadful sight. The captain was tied to the wheel, with a crucifix bound to his hands. He was dead. There was no one else on board — not a single sailor, living or dead.

The ship is the Demeter, from Varna on the Black Sea. Her only cargo was fifty large wooden boxes filled with earth.

The captain's log tells a story that would freeze anyone's blood. Soon after the ship left Varna, the sailors began to disappear one by one in the night. The men whispered that there was someone — or something — on board. The first mate went mad, swearing that he had seen a tall, thin man who was not one of the crew, and that it had vanished like mist when he attacked it. At last only the captain was left. He tied himself to the wheel so that he could not leave his ship. His last words were these: “He is here. I shall stay at my post until the end. God help me.”

Mina Murray's Journal

10 August. Nobody knows where the dog went. And this morning old Mr Swales was found dead on our seat in the churchyard, his neck broken, with a look of terror on his face.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Mina Murray's Journal: Something on the Cliff
chapters.text:
Mina Murray's Journal

11 August, 3 a.m. No sleep now, so I may as well write. I woke in the night with a horrible feeling of fear. The room was dark, and Lucy's bed was empty. The door was shut, but I had forgotten to lock it. I threw on a shawl and ran out into the street.

There was a bright full moon, with heavy black clouds moving across it. When I reached the bridge, I could see the East Cliff across the harbour and the churchyard on top of it. There, on our favourite seat, half lying down, was a white figure. Then a cloud covered the moon, and I could not see clearly, but I thought something long and black was bending over her. Whether it was a man or an animal, I could not tell.

I ran up the hundred and ninety-nine steps to the church. As I came closer, I called out, “Lucy! Lucy!” and something raised its head. For a moment I saw a white face and red, shining eyes. When I reached the seat, Lucy was alone.

She was asleep, breathing in long, heavy gasps, and she put her hand to her throat as if she were cold. I wrapped my shawl round her and fastened it at the neck with a big safety pin. I must have been clumsy and pricked her with it, because later, at home, I noticed two tiny red marks on her throat, like pinpricks, and a drop of blood on her nightdress.

She had come out in bare feet, so I gave her my shoes and walked home barefoot myself. I put mud on my feet so that no one we met would notice. Luckily we met nobody. Lucy remembers nothing, and I shall say nothing to her mother, who has a weak heart.

14 August. Lucy is growing paler and weaker every day, and the little marks on her throat have not healed. They seem larger, if anything, with white edges. Tonight, when I came back to our room, she was sitting up in bed, asleep, pointing at the window. Outside, in the moonlight, a great bat was flying round and round in circles.

18 August. Today, as we sat on the seat in the churchyard, Lucy suddenly told me a little of that night.

“I don't remember being asleep,” she said dreamily. “I only wanted to be here. I remember dogs howling, and a long, dark thing with red eyes. And then something very sweet and very bitter all around me at the same time. I felt as if I were sinking into deep green water, and my soul seemed to leave my body and float in the air. Then you were shaking me, Mina.”

She laughed as she said it, but I did not like the story at all.

19 August. Joy, joy, joy! At last there is news of my dear Jonathan. A letter has come from a hospital in Budapest. He has been there for six weeks with a violent brain fever, and he is still very weak. I am leaving at once to look after him.

Letter from Mina Harker to Lucy Westenra

Budapest, 24 August

My dearest Lucy,

I found Jonathan so thin and pale, and so weak. He remembers nothing of the past few months, or he says he doesn't. The nurse told me that in his fever he raved about wolves and blood and ghosts, and other things too dreadful to repeat.

Yesterday he called me to him and put his hand on his notebook.

“Mina,” he said, “I have had a great shock. When I try to think of it, my head spins, and I don't know if it was all real or the dreams of a madman. The secret is here, and I do not want to know it. Keep this book. Read it if you like, but never tell me what is in it — unless some solemn duty makes me go back to those bitter hours.”

Lucy, we were married this afternoon, here by his hospital bed. Afterwards I wrapped up his notebook, tied it with a ribbon and sealed it with wax, using my wedding ring as the seal. I promised him I would never open it unless it was for his sake.

Be happy, dear, as I am happy now.

Your loving Mina Harker

Lucy Westenra's Diary

Hillingham, London, 25 August. Another bad night. Something was scratching and flapping at the window, and I seem to remember a voice calling me. I woke with my throat sore and a terrible weakness, as if all the strength had been drained out of me. When Arthur came to lunch, he looked quite upset when he saw me, and I hadn't the spirit to try to be cheerful.

Letter from Arthur Holmwood to Dr Seward

31 August

My dear Jack,

I want you to do me a favour. Lucy is ill — not with any illness that anyone can name, but she looks awful and gets worse every day. I have told her I shall ask you to see her, and although she hesitated at first (I know why, old fellow), she agreed. Please come to lunch at Hillingham tomorrow.

I am in an agony of worry. Come.

Arthur

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Dr Seward's Diary: The Strange Illness
chapters.text:
Dr Seward's Diary

2 September. I have examined Lucy. She is pale and weak — she has lost a great deal of blood, it seems to me — and yet I can find no cause. There is no wound, no disease, nothing. I am completely puzzled, so I have written to my old teacher, Professor Abraham Van Helsing of Amsterdam. He knows more about strange diseases than anyone else in the world.

3 September. Van Helsing came, examined Lucy, and joked with her until she laughed. But when we were alone, his face was very grave.

“This is no joke, my friend John,” he said. “It may be life or death, or even more.”

“What do you mean?” I asked.

He only shook his head. “I must think. Send me news every day, and if there is a change, telegraph me at once.”

7 September. The telegram from Hillingham came this morning: Lucy was much worse. Van Helsing and I went straight there. Her face was as white as chalk, her lips were pale, and her gums had drawn back from her teeth. She was breathing with great difficulty.

“There is no time to lose,” said Van Helsing. “She will die simply from lack of blood. We must do a transfusion at once. Which of us — you or me?”

At that moment the doorbell rang, and Arthur rushed in.

“Is it too late?” he cried. “What can I do? I would give my last drop of blood to save her.”

Van Helsing looked at him and smiled. “Young man, I do not ask as much as that — not the last!”

The operation was quickly done. Arthur's healthy blood flowed into Lucy's veins, and as it did, a little colour came back into her cheeks. It was wonderful to see. When Arthur had gone, I noticed Van Helsing studying a narrow black velvet band that Lucy wore round her throat. He moved it gently aside. Underneath were two small holes, red at the centre, white at the edges.

“Well?” he said.

“I don't know what to make of it,” I admitted.

He said nothing more, but that night he left for Amsterdam, “to look at some books,” and he told me to sit up beside her all night and not to close my eyes for a moment.

11 September. Van Helsing is back, and he has brought a large box of white flowers.

“These are for you, Miss Lucy,” he said.

“For me? Oh, Professor!” she laughed — and then she made a face. “But these are only common garlic flowers! Are you playing a joke on me?”

“No jokes,” he said sternly. “I never joke. These flowers are medicine.” He rubbed them all over the window frames and the door, and he made a wreath of them and put it round her neck himself. “Take care you do not take this off. And tonight do not open the window or the door, even if the room feels stuffy.”

Lucy promised, and that night she slept peacefully.

13 September. This morning, when we arrived, Lucy's mother met us in the hall, smiling. “You will be pleased,” she said. “Lucy's room was so stuffy last night, with all those horrible flowers, that I took them away and opened the window to let in some fresh air.”

Van Helsing went grey. When she had gone, he sat down and hid his face in his hands. It was the first time I had ever seen him lose control.

“God! God! What have we done, what has this poor thing done, that fate is so cruel to us? Her own mother, meaning only good, is killing her!” Then he stood up. “Come. We must fight.”

Lucy was as white as death again. This time Van Helsing gave her my blood, and a few days later his own. Each time she grew a little stronger, and each time, somehow, it was lost again.

17 September. At the asylum, Renfield has been very strange. Two nights ago he escaped. We found him at the old chapel door at Carfax, the empty house next door, pressing himself against it and talking to someone inside.

“I am here to do your bidding, Master,” he was saying. “I am your slave, and you will reward me, because I shall be faithful.”

Tonight he broke out of his room again and came at me with a knife. He cut my wrist before the attendants dragged him away. But the worst thing was what I saw when I turned round. Renfield was lying on his stomach on the floor, licking up, like a dog, the blood that had dripped from my wrist.

“The blood is the life!” he kept repeating. “The blood is the life!”

I am exhausted. Van Helsing is in Amsterdam again tonight, but Lucy, I am sure, is safe with her garlic flowers.

18 September. Van Helsing's telegram, sent yesterday afternoon, asked me to spend the night at Hillingham without fail, to see that the flowers were in their place. Through some mistake it was delivered to the wrong address. It reached me only this morning.

Lucy has been alone all night.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Dr Seward's Diary: Lucy
chapters.text:
Memorandum left by Lucy Westenra, night of 17 September

I am writing this down so that nobody may get into trouble because of me. I am alone, and I am afraid.

I went to bed as Dr Van Helsing told me, with the flowers round my neck. Soon I heard a flapping at the window, like the noise I heard at Whitby. Then a dog — or something like a dog — began to howl outside.

Mother came in. She said she was frightened and could not sleep, and she got into bed beside me. Suddenly there was a crash. The window broke, the blind blew back in the wind, and there in the gap was the head of a great grey wolf. Mother screamed. In her terror she grabbed at the wreath round my neck and tore it away. Then she fell back on the pillow. Her heart had stopped. She was dead.

The room seemed to fill with tiny specks, like dust, spinning round and round in the moonlight. I could not move. The maids came, and I sent them to the dining room to drink a glass of wine to calm themselves. They have not come back. I have just been down to look: they are lying on the floor, fast asleep. Someone had put something in the wine.

The air is full of those specks again. I hear the howling. I shall hide this paper in my dress, where they will find it when I am dead. God keep me!

Dr Seward's Diary

18 September. Van Helsing and I arrived together. Nobody answered the bell, and we had to break in through a back window. Lucy's mother lay dead under a white sheet. Lucy was beside her, barely breathing, her throat bare, the two little wounds open and horrible.

We needed another man's blood, and once again help came at the right moment. Quincey Morris had come to ask after Lucy, and he gave his blood without a word. Afterwards he took me aside.

“Jack,” he said, “out on the plains of South America I once saw a horse die in a single night. One of those big bats they call vampires had got at her. What took the blood out of Lucy?”

I could not answer him.

20 September. The end is near. Arthur came this afternoon and has been sitting by her bed. Lucy sleeps most of the time, and she is changing in a way I cannot describe. Her gums have pulled back, and her teeth look longer and sharper than before. In her sleep her breathing becomes heavy and her mouth opens.

Towards evening she opened her eyes, which were dull and hard, and said in a soft, sweet voice I had never heard her use before:

“Arthur! Oh, my love, I am so glad you have come! Kiss me!”

Arthur bent eagerly towards her. But Van Helsing caught him by the collar and threw him back across the room with a strength I would not have believed he had.

“Not for your life!” he said. “Not for your living soul, and hers!”

For a moment a look of pure rage passed over Lucy's face, and her sharp teeth snapped together. Then her eyes closed. When they opened again, they were her own gentle eyes. She reached out a thin white hand and took Van Helsing's.

“My true friend,” she whispered, “and his! Oh, guard him, and give me peace!”

“I swear it,” he said solemnly.

Then Arthur held her hand, and she smiled at him, and soon after that her breathing stopped.

“It is all over,” I said. “She is dead.”

Van Helsing shook his head. “No, not yet, my friend. It is only the beginning.”

When I asked him what he meant, he would only say, “We can do nothing yet. Wait and see.”

Lucy was buried in the family tomb at Hampstead, beside her mother. In death she was more beautiful than ever, and Arthur wept over her like a child.

From the Westminster Gazette, 25 September

A HAMPSTEAD MYSTERY. In the last few days several small children have disappeared from their homes near Hampstead Heath. Each one was found the next morning, weak and pale, with a tiny wound in the throat. All the children tell the same story. They went for a walk with a “bloofer lady” — the children's way of saying “beautiful lady”.

Dr Seward's Diary

26 September. I showed Van Helsing the newspaper. He read it twice and then looked at me in silence.

“Well?” he said. “What do you make of it?”

“Something has bitten those children,” I said. “The same thing that made the holes in poor Lucy's throat, I suppose.”

“Then you are wrong,” he said. “It is worse — far, far worse.”

“What do you mean?”

He sat down heavily and spoke very quietly.

“Those wounds,” he said, “were made by Lucy herself.”

chapters.title: Chapter 8. Dr Seward's Diary: Peace for Lucy
chapters.text:
Dr Seward's Diary

27 September. I told Van Helsing that this was madness. He did not argue. He simply took me that night to the churchyard at Hampstead, opened the door of the Westenra tomb with a key, and unscrewed the lid of Lucy's coffin by candlelight.

The coffin was empty.

“Grave robbers,” I said weakly.

He did not answer. We waited outside among the yew trees until dawn. Just before sunrise I saw something white moving between the graves towards the tomb. Then it was gone.

The next day we went back, and this time Lucy was in her coffin. She was lovelier than when she died, with pink cheeks and lips as red as blood. Van Helsing pulled back her lip with his finger. Her sharp teeth gleamed.

“Now do you believe?” he asked. “She is Un-Dead — a vampire. She was bitten by a vampire, and now she has become one herself. At night she leaves her tomb to drink the blood of children. Every victim she kills will become a vampire too. Unless we stop her, there is no end to it.”

“And how can we stop her?” I asked. My mouth was dry.

“There is only one way. We drive a wooden stake through her heart, cut off her head, and fill her mouth with garlic. Then she will be truly dead, and her soul will be free.”

I felt sick. “And Arthur?” I asked.

“Arthur must see it with his own eyes,” said Van Helsing. “She was to be his wife. We cannot do this without him.”

29 September. We told Arthur and Quincey everything. Arthur's face went white with fury. But at last they both agreed to come and see for themselves.

At midnight the four of us stood in the dark tomb. Van Helsing opened the coffin again. It was empty. Arthur stared at it without a word.

Van Helsing closed the tomb. Then he crumbled up a holy wafer — the bread used in church at Communion — mixed it into a paste and pressed it into the cracks round the door.

“Now she cannot go back in,” he said. “Hide, and watch.”

We waited in the cold, still night. At last, far down the path between the yew trees, we saw a white figure coming towards us. It was a woman in a white burial dress, and she carried something dark in her arms. When the moon came out from behind a cloud, we saw her face.

It was Lucy. And yet it was not Lucy. Her sweetness had turned into a hard, heartless cruelty. Fresh blood ran from her lips down the front of her dress. In her arms was a small child, crying softly.

When she saw us, she snarled like an angry cat. Then she saw Arthur, and her face changed. She dropped the child on the ground without a second look and walked towards him with her arms open.

“Come to me, Arthur,” she said in a soft, sweet voice. “Leave these others and come to me. My arms are hungry for you. Come, and we can rest together. Come, my husband, come!”

Arthur took a step forward, as if in a dream. But Van Helsing jumped between them, holding up a small gold crucifix. Lucy drew back with a hiss. Her face was full of rage — the red eyes, the bloody mouth, the twisted lips. If ever a face meant death, hers did at that moment.

“Answer me, my friend,” said Van Helsing to Arthur. “Shall I go on with my work?”

Arthur fell to his knees and covered his face. “Do what you must,” he groaned. “Nothing could be worse than this.”

Van Helsing removed some of the paste from the tomb door. Lucy — a real body, as solid as ours — slipped through a crack no wider than the edge of a knife and disappeared inside.

30 September. We came back at noon, when vampires have no power. Lucy lay in her coffin as before, horrible in her beauty. Van Helsing took out a sharp wooden stake and a heavy hammer.

“It must be Arthur,” he said gently. “It must be the hand of one who loved her. Then she will be free.”

Arthur took the stake and the hammer. His hand did not tremble. He placed the point over her heart and struck with all his might.

The thing in the coffin twisted and screamed. Its sharp teeth bit through its lips, and red foam came from its mouth. But Arthur never stopped. He struck again and again until at last the body lay still.

The cruel, terrible thing in the coffin was gone. There lay Lucy as we had known her, her face full of sweetness and peace. Arthur bent down and kissed her.

Outside, the sun was shining and the birds were singing.

“My friends,” said Van Helsing, “one part of our work is done. But a greater task remains. We must find the creature who made her what she was, and destroy him. Will you help me?”

One by one we took his hand and swore to do it.

“But where do we start?” asked Quincey.

Van Helsing smiled grimly. “Among Lucy's letters, I found some from a friend of hers, a Mrs Mina Harker. Her husband came home from a journey to the East very ill, raving about wolves and blood. Tomorrow, I go to see her.”

chapters.title: Chapter 9. Mina Harker's Journal: The Hunters Join Forces
chapters.text:
Mina Harker's Journal

22 September. Jonathan and I came up to London today for the funeral of dear old Mr Hawkins. It has been a week of death: my poor Lucy is gone too, and her mother. Afterwards we walked down Piccadilly, arm in arm, and I was thinking how much better Jonathan looked, when suddenly he gripped my arm so hard that it hurt.

“My God!” he whispered.

He was staring at a tall, thin man with a beaked nose, a black moustache and a pointed beard, who was watching a pretty girl in a carriage. The man's face was hard and cruel, and his big white teeth looked all the whiter because his lips were so red.

“Do you see who it is?” said Jonathan. His face was white with terror. “It is the Count! But he has grown young. My God, if I only knew! If I only knew!”

I took him home at once, and he slept for hours. I am frightened, and I have made a decision. I am going to break the seal and read his journal. I must know what this terrible thing is.

24 September. I have read it all. If even half of it is true, then Lucy's death and that man in Piccadilly are part of the same horror. I have typed out a copy of the journal on my typewriter, in case it is ever needed.

1 October. Professor Van Helsing came to see me today. He asked me about our time in Whitby. I told him everything — the sleepwalking, the figure on the seat, the marks on her throat. Then I gave him my typed copy of Jonathan's journal. When he had read it, he took both my hands.

“Madam Mina,” he said, “there is light here, and much of it. Your husband is not mad. Every word in this book is true. I swear it.”

When Jonathan heard this, he was a new man. “I was ill because I doubted,” he said. “I did not know whether to trust my own senses. Now that I know, I am not afraid — not even of him.”

Van Helsing smiled. “So! Then we have work to do.”

2 October. We are all staying with Dr Seward, whose asylum stands right beside Carfax. Last night Dr Seward let me listen to his phonograph diary. To hear the story of Lucy's last days in his voice was terrible, and I cried. Then I typed it all out. Today we have put all our papers together in order. For the first time, we can see the whole picture. The fifty boxes of earth from the Demeter were sent from Whitby to Carfax. The Count is next door.

3 October. This evening we all sat round a table in Dr Seward's study, and Van Helsing told us what we are fighting.

“The vampire is as strong as twenty men,” he said, “and he is clever, with the cunning of centuries. He can command the wolf, the rat, the bat, the fog and the storm. He can change into a wolf or a bat, or into mist. He casts no shadow and has no reflection in a mirror. But he has limits too. He cannot enter a house unless someone inside invites him in. His power ends at sunrise. He must rest in the earth of his own land — and that is why he brought those boxes. He fears garlic, the crucifix and the holy wafer. If we find every box and make it holy, he will have nowhere to hide.”

At that moment there was a loud bang. Mr Morris had fired his pistol through the open window. “Sorry,” he said, “but there was a big bat sitting on the window sill, listening to every word.”

The men decided, very kindly, that I must take no further part in the hunt. It is too dangerous for a woman, they say. I agreed, but my heart sank.

Dr Seward's Diary

3 October. Before we set off, Renfield sent for me. He spoke calmly and sensibly, like a gentleman, and begged me to let him leave the asylum tonight. I refused. He looked at me with real despair.

“You will be sorry for this,” he said quietly. “Perhaps more sorry than you know.”

At midnight we broke into Carfax. The chapel was thick with dust and smelt of old blood and death. Against one wall stood the boxes of earth. We counted them. There were only twenty-nine. The rest had been taken away. As we stood there, the floor began to move, and we saw that it was covered with rats — thousands of them, their little eyes shining in the light of our lamps. Arthur blew his whistle, and three terriers he had brought ran in and drove them back. We put a piece of holy wafer in each box, and left.

Mina Harker's Journal

4 October. Last night, after the men went out, I felt strangely tired and heavy. Then I seemed to dream. A thin white mist was creeping under the door of our room. It grew thicker and thicker, until it stood like a pillar of cloud in the middle of the floor. And at the top of the cloud, looking down at me, were two red eyes — exactly like the eyes Lucy once told me about.

chapters.title: Chapter 10. Dr Seward's Diary: The Mark on Mina's Forehead
chapters.text:
Dr Seward's Diary

5 October. Early this morning Renfield was found on the floor of his room in a pool of blood. His back was broken and his face was terribly crushed. He knew he was dying, and he wanted to talk.

“He came to my window in the fog,” he whispered. “He promised me rats — rats, rats, rats! Hundreds, thousands, millions of them, every one a life. And dogs and cats too. All lives! All red blood, with years of life in it! He would give me all of them, he said, if I would fall down and worship him. So I called him Lord and Master, and I let him in.”

He stopped for breath. Van Helsing's face had gone grey.

“Then Mrs Harker came to see me yesterday,” Renfield went on. “She was pale — like tea when you've poured too much water in it. I don't like pale people. I knew then that he had been taking the life out of her. Just now, when he came again, I tried to stop him. I took hold of him. But his eyes burned me, and he threw me down like a rag.” His voice became a whisper. “He is in there now. With her.”

We ran. The Harkers' door was locked. Arthur and Quincey threw themselves against it, and it burst open.

On the bed lay Jonathan, breathing heavily, in a deep, unnatural sleep. Mina knelt beside him in her white nightdress. And next to her stood a tall, thin man in black. With his left hand he held both her hands, and with his right he gripped the back of her neck and forced her face against his bare chest. A thin stream of blood was running from a cut there. Her white nightdress was stained red. It was like a child forcing a kitten's nose into a saucer of milk.

The Count turned. His eyes blazed with hellish fire, and blood dripped from his lips. He threw Mina back onto the bed and sprang at us. But Van Helsing was ready. He held up an envelope containing the holy wafer, and the Count stopped as if he had hit a wall. Step by step we moved forward, holding up our crucifixes, and step by step he moved back. Then a black cloud covered the moon. When Quincey lit a match, there was nothing in the room but a faint mist, slipping out under the door.

Mina gave a scream so wild and full of despair that I shall hear it until I die. She covered her face with her bloody hands.

“Unclean! Unclean!” she sobbed. “I must touch him or kiss him no more.”

Jonathan woke up and understood at once. He took her in his arms. His hair, I noticed in the morning, had turned almost white.

Later Mina told us the rest. Three times the Count had come to her while we were out hunting him. That night he had laughed at her and told her that from now on she would come whenever he called — across land or sea. Then he had cut open a vein in his chest and made her drink. “Flesh of my flesh,” he had said, “blood of my blood.”

At sunrise Van Helsing touched her forehead with a piece of holy wafer. At once there was a hiss like red-hot metal in water, and Mina screamed. When he took the wafer away, it had burned a red mark into her skin.

She fell to her knees. “Unclean! Even God turns away from me!”

“Not for ever,” said Van Helsing gently. “When he is destroyed, that mark will go. I promise you.”

Jonathan had already traced the missing boxes to houses the Count had bought across London. We found them in Mile End and Bermondsey and made them all holy. The last nine were in a house in Piccadilly. We broke in and found eight. One was missing. Then we waited for the Count.

He came in the afternoon. He moved like a panther. Jonathan rushed at him with his great Indian knife. The Count jumped back just in time, and the blade only cut his coat. A bundle of banknotes and a stream of gold coins fell to the floor. The Count's face was horrible: a greenish-yellow colour, with burning eyes and the red scar on the forehead where Jonathan's shovel had struck him in the castle. When Van Helsing raised the crucifix, the Count dived under Jonathan's arm, grabbed a handful of gold from the floor and leapt through the window. When we looked out, he was standing unhurt in the yard below.

“You think you can defeat me,” he called up at us, “you, with your pale faces all in a row, like sheep in a butcher's shop! You shall be sorry yet, each one of you! My revenge has only just begun. I have centuries ahead of me, and time is on my side. Your girls that you all love are mine already. And through them, you shall be mine too.”

Then he was gone.

“He is afraid,” said Van Helsing quietly. “Why did he take the money? Because he means to travel. He has one box left, and he will run with it. Back to his castle, where he is strongest.”

chapters.title: Chapter 11. Mina Harker's Journal: The Chase to the East
chapters.text:
Mina Harker's Journal

6 October. Just before dawn I woke Jonathan and asked him to bring the Professor. I had had an idea.

“I want you to hypnotise me,” I told Van Helsing. “Do it now, before the sun rises. I think the Count's mind and mine are joined. Perhaps I can see what he sees.”

He made slow movements with his hands in front of my face, and my eyes grew heavy. I remember nothing more, but Jonathan wrote down what I said.

“Where are you?” Van Helsing asked.

“I do not know. It is all strange to me. All is dark.”

“What do you hear?”

“I can hear water. Little waves, lapping. And men shouting. Chains are rattling. Something heavy is falling. The ship is moving.”

As I spoke, the sun rose, and I woke up.

“A ship!” cried Van Helsing. “He is leaving England.”

Within a few hours Arthur and Quincey had searched the shipping records and the docks. The ship was the Czarina Catherine, which had sailed that morning for Varna, on the Black Sea. A tall, thin man with very red lips and sharp teeth had brought a large box on board himself, just before she sailed.

“He thinks he has escaped,” said Van Helsing. “But a ship takes three weeks to reach Varna. We can go across Europe by train in three days. We shall be waiting for him.”

That evening I asked the men to make me a promise.

“If I begin to change,” I said, “if I become like Lucy, you must kill me. Swear it. And you, Jonathan, must do it with your own hand.”

They swore, one by one. Then I asked Jonathan to read the burial service over me, as if I were already dead. I wanted to hear it while I could still understand it. He read it in a shaking voice, and every man in the room was in tears.

15 October, Varna. We have been here for three days, waiting. Every morning at sunrise the Professor hypnotises me, and every morning I give the same answer: “Water lapping. The wind in the sails.” The ship is still at sea.

But I am changing. I sleep more in the day and less at night. I eat little. And my teeth — I have caught Van Helsing looking at them. He thinks I do not notice.

28 October. A telegram from Lloyd's, the shipping office in London. The Czarina Catherine has arrived — not at Varna, but at Galatz, far up the River Danube. The Count has tricked us. He knew we were waiting.

“How could he know?” asked Arthur.

I knew the answer, and it filled me with horror. “Through me,” I said. “If I can see his mind, he can see mine. Everything you say in front of me, he hears.”

Afterwards they spoke more carefully in front of me. But Van Helsing believed that the Count, now that he felt safe, had closed his mind to mine, so that we could not follow him through it. So they let me help with the maps, because, as the Professor said, I had the clearest brain of us all. I studied the rivers, the roads and the railways. The Count's box would not go by road from Galatz — it would be too easy to stop. It would go by boat, up the River Sereth and then up the Bistritza, which runs close to the Borgo Pass. And from there, the Szgany would carry it by cart to the castle.

“Our dear Madam Mina is our teacher again,” said Van Helsing. “Our eyes have been blind, but now we see.”

We have made our plan. Jonathan and Arthur will follow the river in a fast steam launch. Dr Seward and Mr Morris will ride along the bank on horseback, in case the box is taken ashore. And the Professor and I will go by carriage straight to the Borgo Pass, to reach the castle first.

Jonathan kissed me goodbye at the station. He has a great Indian knife at his belt, and a look in his eyes that I have never seen before.

“Now let the Count beware,” he said. “The time has come.”

2 November. We are driving towards the mountains. The Professor says I am a wonderful guide, and it is true: I seem to know the roads, although I have never been here. This morning, under hypnosis, my answer was different.

“I can hear water close to me,” I said, “and wolves howling. Somewhere above me, I can hear the wind. And there are men's voices, speaking a language I do not know.”

The Professor's face grew very grave when he heard. The Count is close to home now. And so are we.

chapters.title: Chapter 12. Memorandum and Journal: The Last Sunset
chapters.text:
Memorandum by Abraham Van Helsing

5 November. Snow is falling, and we are near the Borgo Pass. Madam Mina sleeps almost all day now and eats nothing. Her eyes have a hard light in them that frightens me.

Before it grew dark, I drew a circle around Madam Mina on the ground, and in the circle I crumbled pieces of the holy wafer. I asked her to step out of it. She tried — and she could not. My heart was glad, because I knew that if she could not cross the circle, none of the creatures we feared could cross it either.

At midnight the horses began to scream. The snow was swirling round us, and out of it came three shapes — the same three women that Jonathan saw in the castle, with red lips and sharp white teeth. They came close to the circle and smiled at Madam Mina, and their sweet, terrible voices said, “Come, sister. Come to us. Come!”

She looked at me in horror, and in her eyes I saw that she was still herself. They could not cross the circle, and she would not cross it. At dawn they went away. The horses were dead.

When the sun was high, I left her safe inside the circle and climbed to the castle alone. Down in the old chapel I found the three women in their tombs. They were so beautiful that my hand almost failed me. But I remembered Lucy, and I did my butcher's work. With each one there was a scream, and then, as I watched, the body crumbled into dust. I found one more great tomb, with a single word cut into the stone: DRACULA. I placed a piece of holy wafer inside it, so that he could never rest there again.

Mina Harker's Journal

6 November. The Professor and I waited on a high rock above the road. The sun was sinking towards the mountain tops, and wolves were gathering in the snow below.

Through the field glasses I saw them: a group of Szgany riding as fast as they could, with a cart in the middle. On the cart was a great wooden box. From the south two horsemen were racing towards them — Dr Seward and Mr Morris. From the north came two more: Jonathan and Arthur, who had left their boat and found horses.

In a few minutes the sun would set, and the Count would rise from the box with all his power.

“Halt!” shouted Jonathan.

The Szgany drew their knives and closed round the cart. The four men raised their rifles. Then Jonathan pushed his horse straight into the crowd, jumped onto the cart, and with superhuman strength threw the box to the ground. From the other side Quincey fought his way through, though I saw a knife flash and strike him, and blood running from his side.

Together they broke open the lid. The Count lay in the earth, as pale as a waxwork. His red eyes looked up at the setting sun, and the look of hate in them turned to triumph.

But at that moment Jonathan's great knife flashed and cut through his throat, and Quincey's knife plunged deep into his heart.

It was like a miracle. Before our eyes, almost in a breath, the whole body crumbled into dust and vanished. I shall be glad for the rest of my life that, at the very last moment, there was a look of peace on that face — such peace as I never imagined it could hold.

The Szgany turned their horses and rode away without a word. The wolves slipped back into the trees.

Mr Morris had fallen in the snow, pressing his hand to his side. Blood was running through his fingers. I ran to him, and he took my hand and smiled at me.

“I am only too happy to have been of service,” he said. “Oh, God! It was worth dying for. Look! Look!”

He was pointing at me. The last red light of the sun fell on my face, and the men turned to stare.

“Now God be thanked,” said Quincey, “that all has not been in vain! See! The snow is not more spotless than her forehead! The curse has passed away!”

The red mark had gone. The men fell on their knees in the snow, and with one voice they said, “Amen.” And with a smile, in silence, Quincey died — a brave and gallant gentleman.

Note by Jonathan Harker

Seven years ago we all went through the flames. Today our little boy has his birthday. He was born on the same day that Quincey Morris died, and his name is Quincey. Arthur and Dr Seward are both happily married.

This summer we travelled to Transylvania and stood once more before the old castle. It looked just the same: high and grey and empty above the terrible valley. Among all our papers there is hardly a single real document — only typed pages and diaries. Who would ever believe such a wild story?

Van Helsing lifted our boy onto his knee.

“We want no proofs,” he said. “We ask nobody to believe us. One day this boy will know what a brave and gallant woman his mother is. Later he will understand how some men loved her so much that they dared everything for her sake.”
